title: Review - Top Hat at Chichester Festival Theatre
transcript: Hello and welcome to Theater Reviews with Paul 7. I'm here at the Chichester Festival Theater Brasserie enjoying a meal before going to see Top Hat. Cheers. [Music] Every year I look forward to the Chichester Festival Theater musical. Among the first class revivals of recent years have been Oliver, South Pacific, Crazy for You with the incomparable Charlie Stamp, and Gypsy with Emldda Ston. This year they've chosen Top Hat, and it does not disappoint. There's already an extensive UK tour book for it, so you'll have the chance to see for yourself. Keep watching, and I'll tell you why you shouldn't miss it. But first, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. Once again, Chichester have put together a mouthwatering feast. And I'm not talking about the lovely meal I had in the brassery before the show. Top Hat is primarily a tap dance show. It was written for Fred a stair after all. And the dancing here is top of the tree. Choreographed as well as directed by the great Kathleen Marshall who is responsible for the London hit Anything Goes. The solo dancers, the what you might call Fred and Ginger numbers, and the chorus line work are all masterclasses in how it should be done. The sound of the tap is music in itself and 16 dancers or thereabouts combining to stamp the floor at the same time is explosive. The discipline especially the chorus lines is genuinely awesome as arm in-armm they make a circular movement all the while high kicking. Miss Marshall's choreography is exuberant, uplifting and joyous. A brief word about the story. A worldclass tap dancer called Jerry falls in love with a woman called Dale. But owing to a misunderstanding, she thinks his he's his friend Horus, husband of her friend Match. Spoiler alert, it all works out in the end. So then there's the music. Irvin Berlin wrote 1500 songs throughout a long career, but the five he wrote for the original film show him at his peak and extending his ability to write songs that serve the story. No strings establishes the carefree character of Jerry as well as his prowess as a tap dancer. Isn't this a lovely day starts with Jerry and Dale in a standoff but shows her increasing attachment to him as the song progresses. Cheek to cheek, the centerpiece of the musical shows Jerry seducing Dale through the power of dance. A true representation of the saying, "Dance is the vertical expression of a horizontal desire with climactic moments as he swings her through the air." And uh then there are the two big chorus line numbers top up white tie tails and the picolino which end the first act and begin the second in the stage version. All praise to Steven Ridley and the 10piece Orchestra for their swinging versions. Top Hat, released in cinemas in 1935, only became a stage musical in 2011 when it was adapted by Matthew White and Howard Jakes. There are many more Berlin tunes added. Quite a few plundered from other Fred and Ginger movies. Um, and so you get putting on the putting on the Ritz, I'm putting all my eggs in one basket. uh let yourself go and uh let's face the music and dance. Keep watching and I'll tell you about the cast, including a true musical star and I'll let you know about a dramatic incident on the press night just after the show began. I'm Paul 7 Lewis and I'm talking about Top Hat at Chichester Festival Theater. The six principles are superb. The ensemble is wonderful. The hardest job goes to Philip Atmore. How to step into the shoes of Fred a stair. Not to mention that the show itself refers to him as a top draw dancer. And unlike the great man, he has to perform live. The good news is he may not be quite Fred a stair who is, but he is a likable lead and an excellent dancer. Lucy St. Louis is the full package as Dale. She has a powerful singing voice, acts well, and dances beautifully. For me, she was a revelation, the star of the show. And I shouldn't be surprised because she's already played Glender in Wicked and Christine in The Phantom of the Opera. You may have seen her perform at the Platinum Party at the Palace. Clive Carter and Salan Triplet as Horus and Match provide a weight of experience and a huge dose of comedy. James Clyde as Horus's servant Bates in various disguises and Alex Gibson Giorgio as Alberto, a comical Italian fashion designer and Dale's wouldbe lover also keep the laughs coming. There's a great deal of of funny lines. Maybe corny jokes would be a better description. Now, here's an example. Horus is afraid of flying because the first word you see at an airport on the signs is terminal. But that's very much in the mood of this light comedy, which as I said is about dance first, then music, and only then comedy to fill the gaps. Peter Mintosh's luminous art deco set is very clever. The thrust stage is kept clear for dancing, although there are semic-ircular rises. But at the back, there is a revolve that swiftly takes us from one bedroom to another bedroom to the bar. He along with Ivonne Mills also designed the costumes which have the loose easygoing feel of the 1940s rather than slavishly copying the 1930s style of the film. I left the auditorium on a high and while Top Hat the stage show may not match the perfection of the film uh and that may also be the reason why Crazy for You and uh and Anything Goes seem like they have more of a wow factor because there is no equivalent film to compare them with. Nevertheless, this show is performed live and seeing a group of supremely talented people right there in front of you creating beautiful, athletic, complex dance together to some of the greatest songs ever written. Well, that makes Top Hat at Chester Festival a joy beyond any flickering screen. I give Top Hat four stars. Oh, yes, that incident I mentioned. Well, the overture finished and a line of dancers snaked onto the stage. Suddenly, one fell over, then another, then another. Before they all fell like nine pins, the ensemble left the stage and the show was halted. It may be a record for the shortest time between the show starting and stopping. It turned out, as director Kathleen Marshall came on to explain, the floor was inexplicably wet. Well, stage hands quickly dried it. The show recommenced. The cast stayed upright this time and delivered the musical treat of the summer. [Music] I hope you found this review useful uh and entertaining maybe. Uh if you did, why not subscribe to this channel and you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. You can also read my reviews and uh my roundups of other critics reviews at my website theater.reviews and of course you can follow me on various social media. Thank you for watching.
